passages.title: The Line That Changed Shopping
passages.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

paragraphs.text: In the autumn of 1948, a graduate student named Bernard Silver was walking through the engineering building of the Drexel Institute of Technology in Philadelphia when he overheard an unusual conversation. The president of a local food chain had come to ask the dean whether the college might develop a machine capable of reading product information automatically as customers passed through the checkout. Queues in his stores were long, stock records were unreliable, and every price had to be keyed in by hand. The dean listened politely and turned the request down. Silver, however, could not let the idea go. He repeated it to a friend and fellow student, Norman Joseph Woodland, and within weeks the two men had begun work on a problem that would occupy them, on and off, for the next quarter of a century.

Progress was slow, and in early 1949 Woodland took the unusual step of leaving the Institute altogether. He moved into his grandfather's apartment in Florida, sold a small quantity of shares, and devoted himself to the problem full time. The breakthrough, according to the account he gave for the rest of his life, came on a beach. Sitting in a deckchair and thinking about Morse code, which he had memorised as a Boy Scout, he pushed four fingers into the sand and drew them towards himself, leaving a set of grooves behind. If the dots and dashes of Morse could be stretched downwards into thin and thick lines, he reasoned, a machine might be able to tell them apart. Moments later he swept his hand round in a circle, producing a pattern of rings. A circular symbol, unlike a row of lines, could be read from any direction - a considerable advantage at a busy checkout, where an assistant could not be expected to line up every package the same way.

Woodland and Silver applied for a patent in October 1949, and it was granted three years later. Their invention was not, at that stage, a set of parallel bars but a bullseye: a series of concentric circles of varying width. The difficulty was that no technology existed to read it cheaply. Their prototype used a five-hundred-watt incandescent bulb and a light-sensitive tube of the kind used to read the soundtracks on cinema film. The apparatus filled a desk, had to be operated in a darkened room, and produced so much heat that the paper carrying the symbol began to smoulder. Woodland wrapped the bulb in black paper to control the glare, and worked on. In 1962, with no commercial prospect in sight, the two men sold the patent to the electronics firm Philco for fifteen thousand dollars. It was the only money either of them ever made from the invention. Philco later passed the patent to RCA. Silver died in 1963, at the age of thirty-eight, long before the idea he had overheard came to anything.

The impetus finally came from the retailers themselves. In 1966 the National Association of Food Chains, exasperated by rising labour costs, publicly called on the electronics industry to produce a workable automated checkout. RCA, which now owned the patent, revived the bullseye and installed a system in a Kroger supermarket in Cincinnati in 1972. Shoppers liked it. The printing industry did not. Rotary presses smear ink slightly in the direction of travel, and while a smeared bar can still be measured across its width, a smeared circle becomes an unreadable blur. The trial exposed a flaw that no amount of refinement could correct, and the bullseye was abandoned - not because it cost too much to print, but because it could not be printed reliably enough.

By this time Woodland was working for IBM, and it was an IBM engineer, George Laurer, who produced the answer. Laurer's symbol was rectangular and made up of vertical bars, deliberately shaped so that ink spreading in the direction of printing would not alter the ratios a scanner measured. In the spring of 1973, after three years of deliberation, a committee of grocery executives selected it as the Universal Product Code, the standard still in use today. Fifteen months later, at one minute past eight on the morning of 26 June 1974, a cashier at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, drew a ten-pack of chewing gum across a scanner window and the till registered sixty-seven cents. The packet is now held by the Smithsonian Institution.

Adoption, however, was anything but rapid. A scanning installation cost several thousand dollars per lane, and the saving depended entirely on how many products arrived already marked. Manufacturers, for their part, saw little reason to print codes on packaging until enough shops could read them. The result was a stalemate that took most of a decade to break. By the end of the 1970s only about one per cent of American grocery stores had installed scanners, and one trade journal had already published an article under the title 'The Supermarket Scanner That Failed'. Only in the 1980s, once coded packaging had become the norm rather than the exception, did the technology spread quickly.

What it made possible turned out to be far larger than shorter queues. Because every sale now generated a record of what had been bought, when, and at what price, retailers could track stock in something close to real time, reorder automatically, and analyse demand at the level of the individual item. Whole industries - barcode-based logistics, just-in-time distribution, the scanner-panel market research that supermarkets now sell back to manufacturers - grew out of a symbol originally intended only to shorten a queue. Woodland received the National Medal of Technology in 1992. He is said to have remarked that the hardest part had never been the idea, but the wait.

passages.title: The Return of the Beaver
passages.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The Eurasian beaver, Castor fiber, was once as ordinary a feature of the British landscape as the oak. Its bones turn up in Neolithic rubbish heaps, and its name survives in places from Beverley in Yorkshire to Beverston in Gloucestershire. It was hunted out of existence all the same. Beaver fur is dense enough to be waterproof and was pressed into the felt hats fashionable across Europe for three centuries. The meat was classified by the medieval church as fish, and could therefore be eaten on the many days when meat was forbidden. Most valuable of all was castoreum, a secretion from glands near the tail, used first in medicine and later in perfume. By the sixteenth century the species had disappeared from Britain, and by 1900 no more than 1,200 animals survived in a handful of scattered refuges across the whole of Eurasia.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Its return has been slow and, in Britain, argumentative. A licensed trial began at Knapdale in Argyll in 2009, using animals brought from Norway. A second population, of unknown origin, was found living wild on the River Otter in Devon in 2014 and was allowed to remain under a five-year study; in 2020 those animals were granted permission to stay for good, the first formal restoration of an extinct native mammal to England. Farming organisations objected throughout, and not all of the scientific community was comfortable either. Grace Okoye, a fisheries scientist who advised the Devon study, points out that the effect of dams on migrating salmon and sea trout is still poorly understood. A dam may obstruct adult fish moving upstream in a dry summer, yet the pond behind it shelters juveniles through the same drought. Until somebody has counted fish above and below a series of dams for twenty years, she argues, confident statements in either direction are guesswork rather than science.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: To follow the argument it helps to know why beavers build at all. A beaver is a poor runner and a superb swimmer: on land it is prey, in deep water it is safe. Almost everything it constructs serves one purpose, which is to keep water deep enough to hide the underwater entrance to its lodge and to let it float timber home rather than drag it. A dam is not a house; it is a device for raising the level of the water in front of one. The animals work at night, hauling in branches, stones and mud, and they are triggered almost entirely by sound - it is the noise of running water that makes a beaver build. A dam a metre high may hold back a pond of several hundred square metres, and where a valley is flat a single family will construct a staircase of ten or twelve of them, one behind another.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences for the movement of water have attracted most of the recent research. Helena Marsh, a hydrologist who has monitored instrumented catchments in south-west England for the past decade, describes a beaver-occupied stream as "a set of leaky buckets arranged in series". Rain arriving in a storm is held in the ponds and in the saturated ground around them, then released over hours rather than minutes. In her measurements, the peak flow leaving a beaver reach was on average around thirty per cent lower than the peak entering it, and it arrived some ninety minutes later. Marsh is careful about how far this can be scaled up. The clearest results, she emphasises, come from headwater streams draining only a few square kilometres; on a large lowland river the same structures make little measurable difference, and the popular claim that beavers can defend a city from flooding runs a long way ahead of the evidence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Alan Redfern, a freshwater ecologist, is more interested in what the ponds hold than in what leaves them. Silt washed off arable fields settles behind a dam instead of travelling downstream, and it takes with it the phosphates and nitrates bound to its particles; water leaving a beaver pond is measurably clearer and lower in nutrients than water entering it. Meanwhile the standing water, the dead wood and the sunlit clearings opened up where beavers have felled trees together produce a mosaic of habitats that has become rare in the British countryside. Redfern's surveys at one Devon site recorded a trebling of amphibian numbers within five years of the animals' arrival, together with sharp rises in dragonflies, water beetles, and the birds that feed on them. "A beaver does not simply live in a wetland," he says. "It manufactures one, and everything else moves in."

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Not everyone downstream is grateful. Priya Anand, an agricultural economist, has attempted to put a figure on the other side of the ledger: waterlogged fields taken out of production, blocked field drains and culverts, undermined farm tracks, and orchard and plantation trees ring-barked or brought down. Her argument is less about the total, which she describes as modest when spread across a national economy, than about the way it is distributed. The benefits of a beaver population are shared thinly among everyone who lives downstream, while the costs land on the small number of farmers whose land happens to lie beside the pond. A programme that is inexpensive for society as a whole can still be ruinous for an individual, and Anand maintains that no reintroduction should proceed without a funded compensation scheme agreed in advance.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Tomas Lindqvist, who has spent his career on beaver management in Scandinavia and central Europe, regards the conflict as technical rather than fundamental. Where a pond threatens a road or a field, a pipe can be pushed through the dam with its inlet caged some distance upstream; because the beavers cannot hear the water escaping, they make no attempt to repair the leak, and the pond settles at whatever depth the pipe has been set to hold. Valuable trees can be wrapped in wire mesh, or painted with a mixture of paint and coarse sand which the animals dislike the feel of. In Bavaria a small paid staff of beaver consultants visits landowners and fits such devices free of charge; public support there has remained high for thirty years. Lindqvist's own conclusion is blunt. "The moment the question stops being philosophical and becomes practical, most of the heat goes out of it. Opposition is usually strongest in the places where nobody has yet been shown a remedy."

passages.title: In Praise of Boredom
passages.instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.text: For a state that almost everybody experiences, boredom has attracted remarkably little serious attention. Psychology has produced libraries on anxiety, grief and anger; boredom, until the last two decades, was left largely to novelists. Part of the reason is that, unlike other unpleasant feelings, it is not taken seriously. Nobody is admitted to hospital with it. It is treated as a triviality, a complaint of the idle, and the person who admits to it is generally thought to be confessing a shortcoming of their own. That suspicion has a long history. Medieval monastic writers described acedia, a listless inability to attend to anything, and classed it among the deadly sins; nineteenth-century moralists regarded boredom as evidence of an untrained mind. The assumption in each case was the same. An interesting person is never bored, and the feeling is therefore a verdict on the sufferer rather than on the situation.

Modern researchers begin by clearing away the commonest misunderstanding, which is that boredom means having nothing to do. It does not. A prisoner in solitary confinement has nothing to do; a commuter working through a dull report has a great deal to do. What the two have in common is a mismatch - the wish to be occupied by something, combined with an inability to be occupied by anything available. Boredom is now usually defined as an aversive state of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity, which makes it, awkwardly, a condition of restlessness and inertia at the same time. It is why the bored person paces, checks a phone, opens the fridge and settles to nothing.

How unpleasant is it? In an experiment that has been reported many times since, participants were asked to spend fifteen minutes alone in a bare room with nothing but their own thoughts. The room contained a device that delivered a mild electric shock. In an earlier session every participant had sampled that shock and stated that they would pay money to avoid receiving it again. Left alone, two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women gave themselves at least one shock; one man administered more than a hundred. The finding is usually retold as a curiosity, but it deserves more weight than that. It suggests that undirected attention is not merely dull but genuinely difficult, and that a considerable number of people would rather feel something unpleasant than nothing at all.

Mira Halloran, a psychologist who has spent fifteen years on the subject, thinks the discomfort is precisely the point. She compares boredom to hunger, thirst and pain: states that are unpleasant by design, because their function is to make us act. Hunger does not tell you what to eat, only that you need to eat. Boredom, in her account, is the signal that whatever you are currently doing is failing to occupy you meaningfully, and that your attention would be better spent elsewhere. It is, she says, "the mechanism by which we notice that we are wasting our lives" - an uncomfortable but useful alarm. An organism incapable of boredom would simply continue with whatever it happened to be doing. On this reading, a world that had succeeded in abolishing boredom would be a world that had thrown away one of its more valuable instruments.

The most eye-catching support for the idea comes from laboratory work on creativity. Participants asked to perform a deliberately tedious task - copying numbers out of a telephone directory is the classic version - before being asked to think of unusual uses for an everyday object typically produce more ideas, and stranger ones, than participants who go straight to the second task. The result has been repeated often enough to become a staple of business journalism, usually under a headline advising readers to schedule boredom into the working week. Daniel Weir, a cognitive scientist, regards this literature with impatience. The effects, he points out, are small; several attempted replications have found nothing at all; and the creativity being measured is a laboratory proxy that nobody has shown to predict creative achievement outside the laboratory. That boredom sometimes precedes a good idea does not establish that it produced one. His caution seems to me considerably better founded than the enthusiasm it is aimed at.

There is also a substantial body of evidence pointing the other way. People who score highly on scales of boredom-proneness - a stable tendency to find situations unengaging - report more gambling, more risk-taking, poorer academic results, higher rates of substance use and lower job satisfaction, and one long-running cohort study even found an association with mortality. Taken at face value this looks like a straightforward case against boredom. But boredom-proneness is a trait, not an episode, and that distinction matters more than anything else in the field. The occasional experience of boredom appears to be informative and probably useful. A permanent inability to find anything engaging is a different phenomenon altogether, closer to a symptom than to a signal, and it is to this that the unhappy outcomes attach.

The contemporary worry is that the first is being quietly converted into the second. A phone abolishes the waiting room, the bus queue and the ten minutes before sleep - precisely the intervals in which the mind used to be left to wander. Surveys report rising levels of self-reported boredom among adolescents over the same period in which screen use has climbed, and the temptation to join those two facts into a single sentence is strong. It should be resisted. The data are correlational, self-reports of boredom are notoriously unstable, and the direction of the arrow is anybody's guess, since bored teenagers may simply be reaching for their phones. What can be said more safely is narrower: if boredom is a signal, then a device that reliably suppresses the signal without addressing whatever produced it is doing something that deserves thought.

All of which suggests that the question we normally ask is the wrong one. Parents ask how to stop their children being bored; employers ask how to keep staff engaged; all of us ask what to do when the feeling arrives, and the answer is now almost always a screen. The more useful question is what the feeling is pointing at. Boredom in a lesson may be a fact about the lesson. Boredom on a Sunday afternoon may be information about a life. Treating it as a fault to be corrected - in oneself, in one's children, in one's employees - guarantees only that the message is never read.
